items.title: Kronecker coefficients and the internal tensor product
items.statement:
Fix an integer $n\ge0$ and work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ be
partitions of $n$
([[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]), and let
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ be the tensor product of their complex
Specht modules, a finite-dimensional complex $S_n$-module
([[def-tensor-product-of-complex-representations]],
[[def-column-antisymmetrizer-polytabloid-and-specht-module]]). The
**Kronecker coefficient** $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ of a third partition
$\nu\vdash n$ is the multiplicity of $S^\nu$ in this tensor product:

$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu):=\frac{\dim_{\mathbb C}\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}}{\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu},$$

where $\bigl(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\bigr)_{(S^\nu)}$ is the isotypic
component of type $S^\nu$
([[def-isotypic-component-of-a-completely-reducible-representation]]).

**Well-definedness.** The module $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$ is
finite-dimensional, and $\operatorname{char}\mathbb C=0$ does not divide the
order of the finite group $S_n$, so complex Maschke's theorem gives complete
reducibility
([[thm-maschkes-theorem-for-finite-groups-over-fields-whose-characteristic-does-not-divide-the-group-order]],
[[cor-finite-dimensional-representations-are-completely-reducible-when-char-k-does-not-divide-group-order]],
[[def-completely-reducible-representation]]). The complex Specht modules
$S^\nu$, $\nu\vdash n$, are a complete list of pairwise inequivalent
irreducible $S_n$-modules
([[thm-complex-specht-modules-are-irreducible]],
[[thm-complex-irreducibles-of-symmetric-groups-are-specht-modules]],
[[cor-distinct-specht-modules-are-inequivalent]]). Consequently a decomposition
into irreducibles has the form
$S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu\cong\bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu S^\nu$
with nonnegative integer multiplicities $m_\nu$, and the isotypic component of
type $S^\nu$ is the direct sum of exactly the $m_\nu$ copies of $S^\nu$
appearing in any such decomposition, by
[[thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique]]
(Proof step 2.1 identifies each grouped block with the defining isotypic sum).
In particular
$\dim_{\mathbb C}(S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu)_{(S^\nu)}=m_\nu\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu$
and $\dim_{\mathbb C}S^\nu>0$ because $S^\nu$ is irreducible. Hence
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=m_\nu$ is a nonnegative integer, independent of the chosen
decomposition, and $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ is by definition the multiplicity of
$S^\nu$ in $S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$.

**The internal product.** For partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ call
$$(\lambda,\mu)\longmapsto S^\lambda\otimes_{\mathbb C}S^\mu$$
the **internal (Kronecker) product** of the $S_n$-representations $S^\lambda$
and $S^\mu$. Unlike the outer induction product
$\operatorname{Ind}_{S_a\times S_b}^{S_{a+b}}(S^\alpha\boxtimes S^\beta)$ of
[[thm-outer-littlewood-richardson-rule]], which takes a pair of modules of
degrees $a$ and $b$ to a module of degree $a+b$, the internal product keeps the
rank: both inputs and the output are $S_n$-modules of the same degree $n$. The
two operations are different constructions on different data; the outer product
is mentioned here only for contrast and is not used in this definition.

No form of the Axiom of Choice is used: the tensor product, Maschke's theorem,
the Specht classification and the isotypic decomposition are finite-dimensional
complex representation theory of a finite group.
items.strategy: Complete reducibility comes from complex Maschke applied to the finite-dimensional S_n-module S^lambda (x) S^mu; the classification and pairwise inequivalence of the S^nu make the isotypic component decomposition available. Well-definedness of the multiplicity is canonical: the isotypic component of a completely reducible module is defined as the sum of all irreducible submodules equivalent to S^nu, so it does not depend on a chosen decomposition, and dim S^nu > 0 because S^nu is irreducible. The contrast with the outer product is prose only and creates no logical dependency; the outer induction product is not used. The isotypic-block equality is supplied explicitly by thm-isotypic-decomposition-of-a-completely-reducible-representation-is-unique, Proof step 2.1.
items.axiom_use: None: the argument is finite-dimensional complex representation theory of a finite group and is choice-free (complex Maschke and the Specht classification are choice-free in the cited suppliers).

items.title: Complex Specht modules are self-dual with real-valued characters
items.statement: For every lambda |- n the complex Specht module S^lambda carries a nondegenerate symmetric S_n-invariant bilinear form b(x,y) = sum_T x_T y_T (coefficientwise product in the tabloid basis), so v -> b(v,-) is an isomorphism of C S_n-modules S^lambda -> (S^lambda)^*; equivalently S^lambda is self-dual. Consequently chi^lambda(g^{-1}) = chi^lambda(g), i.e. every irreducible character of S_n is real-valued.
items.strategy: The coefficientwise product b is symmetric, bilinear and invariant because S_n permutes the tabloid basis. It is nondegenerate on the tabloid module M^lambda. Every polytabloid has integer tabloid coefficients and is fixed by coefficientwise conjugation; conjugating an arbitrary complex linear combination of these generators gives another such combination, so S^lambda is stable under conjugation; writing H(x,y) = sum_T conj(x_T) y_T for the published invariant Hermitian form (which the previous item proves to be nondegenerate on S^lambda), we have b(x,y) = H(conj(x), y) for x,y in S^lambda, and conj(S^lambda) = S^lambda. For nonzero x in S^lambda, conj(x) is also a nonzero vector of S^lambda, so nondegeneracy of H supplies y in S^lambda with H(conj(x),y) != 0; hence b is nondegenerate on S^lambda. Invariance of b gives equivariance of v -> b(v,-) with the dual action (g.f)(w) = f(g^{-1}w); nondegeneracy plus finite dimension makes it an isomorphism. Finally chi_{(S^lambda)^*}(g) = conj(chi^lambda(g)) by the tensor/dual character theorem, so chi^lambda(g) = chi^lambda(g^{-1}) = conj(chi^lambda(g)) is real.
items.axiom_use: None: the tabloid form, conjugation in the tabloid basis and the character comparison are finite-dimensional and choice-free.

items.title: The Kronecker coefficient is a three-character inner product
items.statement: For all lambda,mu,nu |- n, g(lambda,mu,nu) = <chi^lambda chi^mu, chi^nu> = (1/n!) sum_{sigma in S_n} chi^lambda(sigma) chi^mu(sigma) chi^nu(sigma), where the sum uses the real-valuedness of the irreducible characters (no conjugation on the third factor).
items.strategy: The character of a tensor product is the pointwise product, so S^lambda (x) S^mu has character chi^lambda chi^mu. For a finite-dimensional completely reducible module with character phi the multiplicity of the irreducible character chi^nu equals <phi, chi^nu>, computed by the intertwiner-dimension formula together with the orthonormality of irreducible characters on S_n. Finally chi^nu(g^{-1}) = conj(chi^nu(g)) by the dual-character formula and chi^nu(g^{-1}) = chi^nu(g) by self-duality, so the inner product can be written as the plain average of the triple product.
items.axiom_use: None: finite-dimensional character theory over C.

references.title: Igor Pak and Greta Panova, Bounds on the Kronecker coefficients, arXiv:1406.2988v2 (2014)
references.locator: §2.3, printed pp. 3–4: the triple character formula and full S_3 symmetry; (2.3) is the two-partition conjugation identity.

references.title: I. G. Macdonald, Symmetric Functions and Hall Polynomials, 2nd ed., Oxford University Press 1995

items.title: Kronecker coefficients are nonnegative integers with full S_3 and conjugation symmetries
items.statement: For all lambda,mu,nu |- n: (a) g(lambda,mu,nu) is a nonnegative integer; (b) g(lambda,mu,nu) is invariant under every permutation of lambda,mu,nu; (c) conjugating exactly two of the three partitions preserves the coefficient: g(lambda,mu,nu) = g(lambda',mu',nu) = g(lambda',mu,nu') = g(lambda,mu',nu'). No positive combinatorial rule is asserted.
items.strategy: (a) is the multiplicity definition; the character formula expresses it as a nonnegative integer. (b) follows from the symmetric form of the three-character average together with commutativity of pointwise multiplication and real-valuedness of the three characters. (c) uses S^{lambda'} = S^lambda (x) sgn from the sign-twist/omega item: S^{lambda'} (x) S^{mu'} = (S^lambda (x) S^mu) (x) (sgn (x) sgn) and sgn (x) sgn is the trivial representation, so the tensor product is unchanged; the multiplicity of S^{nu'} (respectively S^nu) in it equals that of S^nu (respectively S^{nu'}) because sgn is one-dimensional, giving the three displayed equalities.

items.title: The internal (Kronecker) product on symmetric functions
items.statement: Let ch: R_S -> Lambda be the Frobenius characteristic, a degree-preserving ring isomorphism from the graded character ring of the symmetric groups onto the stable symmetric-function ring. For f in Lambda^m and g in Lambda^n define f * g := ch( ch^{-1}(f) . ch^{-1}(g) ) if m = n, where the dot is the pointwise (internal tensor) product of class functions, and f * g := 0 if m != n; extend bilinearly. Then * is a degree-preserving, commutative, associative, bilinear product on Lambda with degreewise unit h_n = s_(n) = ch(trivial character of S_n) on Lambda^n (h_0 = 1); the direct sum Lambda has no global unit for *, and for partitions lambda,mu of n, s_lambda * s_mu = sum_nu g(lambda,mu,nu) s_nu.
items.strategy: Closure of R(S_n) under the pointwise product: honest characters of S_n multiply to the character of the tensor product of the corresponding representations, and virtual characters are integral combinations, so the product of two elements of R(S_n) lies in R(S_n). Hence the transport through the graded isomorphism ch is well defined and inherits bilinearity, commutativity and associativity from pointwise multiplication. The Schur expansion follows from ch(chi^lambda) = s_lambda and the definition of g. On Lambda^n the trivial character is the unit for pointwise multiplication, so its characteristic h_n = s_(n) is the internal-product unit. Every element of the graded direct sum has finite degree support; for a degree n outside that support its internal product with the nonzero h_n is zero, so it cannot be a global unit. In particular the ordinary-product unit 1 in degree zero is not a unit for * on positive degrees.
items.axiom_use: None: the transport uses the choice-free Frobenius characteristic isomorphism.

items.title: Power sums diagonalize the internal product
items.statement: For partitions rho,sigma of n one has p_rho * p_sigma = delta_{rho,sigma} z_rho p_rho, where z_rho = prod_i i^{m_i(rho)} m_i(rho)!; consequently s_lambda * s_mu = sum_{nu |- n} g(lambda,mu,nu) s_nu. The internal product of symmetric functions is therefore diagonal in the power-sum basis and has integer structure constants (the Kronecker coefficients) in the Schur basis. Power sums are a basis after extension to Lambda_Q; the integral identity is proved before extending the product.
items.strategy: Expand u_rho=z_rho 1_rho in the orthonormal Specht-character basis: its coefficients chi^lambda(rho) are integers, so u_rho is a virtual character. Its characteristic is p_rho and u_rho u_sigma=delta_(rho,sigma) z_rho u_rho. Apply the integral internal-product definition, then explicitly extend the bilinear product to Q by clearing denominators.

items.title: First-row padding of a partition
items.statement: For a partition alpha and an integer n, define alpha[n] := (n - |alpha|, alpha_1, alpha_2, ...) whenever n >= |alpha| + alpha_1; the displayed sequence is then a partition of n, and below the threshold it is not a partition (the first part is smaller than the second, or negative). The threshold |alpha| + alpha_1 is exact. This notation is neutral: it records no constancy and is shared with the FI-module and representation-stability developments. Read alpha_1=0 for the empty partition and empty[0]=empty. No FI-module generation degree is asserted.
items.strategy: Weak decrease of (n - |alpha|, alpha_1, alpha_2, ...) is equivalent to n - |alpha| >= alpha_1, i.e. n >= |alpha| + alpha_1, because alpha itself is weakly decreasing; conversely n < |alpha| + alpha_1 makes the first entry smaller than alpha_1 (when alpha is nonempty) so the sequence is not a partition. The empty partition case alpha = empty gives alpha[n] = (n).

items.title: Padded Kronecker coefficient sequences
items.statement: Let alpha,beta,gamma be partitions and let n_0 := max{|alpha|+alpha_1, |beta|+beta_1, |gamma|+gamma_1}. For integers n >= n_0 all three padded sequences alpha[n], beta[n], gamma[n] are partitions of n, and one defines g_n(alpha,beta,gamma) := g(alpha[n], beta[n], gamma[n]). Below n_0 the notation is undefined because at least one padded sequence is not a partition. The padded Kronecker coefficient sequence on N is k -> g_(n_0+k)(alpha,beta,gamma), with k >= 0; the size-indexed notation g_n retains its common padding domain. This definition asserts no eventual constancy; Murnaghan stability is a theorem about this sequence proved elsewhere.
items.strategy: On the common domain each alpha[n] is a partition of n by the preceding item, so g_n is the already-defined Kronecker coefficient of three partitions of n; the maximum threshold is exactly where the common domain starts. No well-definedness beyond this is claimed and no limit is taken.

items.title: Littlewood's identity - the internal product against an outer product
items.statement: For partitions lambda |- n, tau |- r and theta |- n - r, Littlewood's identity holds in Lambda^n: s_lambda * (s_tau s_theta) = sum_{alpha |- r, beta |- n-r} c^lambda_{alpha,beta} (s_alpha * s_tau)(s_beta * s_theta), with c^lambda_{alpha,beta} the Littlewood-Richardson coefficient. Both sides have degree n and the sum is finite.
items.strategy: Work with class functions and pass to symmetric functions only at the end. Let H <= S_n be the two-block subgroup S_r x S_{n-r}. By the outer Littlewood-Richardson rule, Ind_H^{S_n}(S^alpha (x) S^beta) = sum_lambda c^lambda_{alpha,beta} S^lambda, so Frobenius reciprocity gives the restriction multiplicity [Res_H chi^lambda : chi^alpha (x) chi^beta] = c^lambda_{alpha,beta}. Frobenius' formula writes the induced character chi^tau o chi^theta at sigma as a sum over cosets of the values at x^{-1} sigma x, and chi^lambda(sigma) = chi^lambda(x^{-1} sigma x) because chi^lambda is a class function. Multiplying pointwise and using the restriction expansion of chi^lambda at every coset term that lies in H turns the product into sum_{alpha,beta} c^lambda_{alpha,beta} Ind_H^{S_n}((chi^alpha . chi^tau) (x) (chi^beta . chi^theta)). Applying the characteristic map, which preserves outer products and sends chi^mu to s_mu, and using that * is defined by transporting pointwise products gives the stated identity.
items.axiom_use: None: induction, Frobenius reciprocity and the outer LR rule are choice-free in the cited suppliers.

items.title: The Kronecker reduction lemma of Pak and Panova
items.statement:
Let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge0$, and let $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$ have lengths at most $\ell$. Read missing parts as zero and put $s:=n-\nu_1$, with $\nu_1=0$ for the empty partition.

**(i)** If $|\lambda_i-\mu_i|>s$ for some $i\le\ell$, then $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=0$.

**(ii)** Otherwise put $\rho:=\lambda\cap\mu$, $\omega:=\lambda\cup\mu$, $\omega_{\ell+1}:=0$, and define
$$\delta_i:=\max\{0,\rho_i-\omega_{i+1}-2s\},\qquad D_j:=\sum_{i=j}^{\ell}\delta_i,\qquad \varphi(\theta)_j:=\theta_j-D_j\quad(1\le j\le\ell).$$
For every partition $\theta$ with at most $\ell$ parts satisfying $\rho_j-s\le\theta_j\le\omega_j$ for each $j$, the image $\varphi(\theta)$ is a partition after deletion of zero parts. In particular $\varphi(\lambda)$ and $\varphi(\mu)$ have a common size $r$, and $\varphi(\nu):=(r-s,\nu_2,\nu_3,\ldots)$ is a partition of $r$. Then
$$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)=g(\varphi(\lambda),\varphi(\mu),\varphi(\nu)),\qquad r\le2s\ell^2.$$

This is a corrected reduction map for the bounded-reduction conclusion of Pak–Panova. It retains their Littlewood–Richardson/Jacobi–Trudi proof route and the same size bound; the map is not the block formula printed in their papers. Delete zero parts in phi(nu), with phi(nu)=empty when r=s=0.
items.strategy: Use Littlewood internal/outer compatibility to obtain the finite LR coefficient identity, expand the third Schur function along the first Jacobi–Trudi row, and prove small-skew LR and inverse-index invariance under Phi(theta)=theta-D with delta_i=max(0,rho_i-omega_(i+1)-2s); prove output partitions and the original r<=2s ell^2 bound separately for ell=1, ell=2 and ell>=3. The complexity-paper block map has a nonpartition output on the explicit first example in Remarks; no coefficient-changing counterexample is claimed.
items.axiom_use: None intended: the argument uses Littlewood's identity, LR/Pieri expansions of symmetric functions, the Jacobi-Trudi identity and finite tableau combinatorics. The authoring stage must confirm that no cited supplier silently assumes the Axiom of Choice.

items.title: Row-gap reduction and conditional k-stability of Kronecker coefficients
items.statement:
Fix $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$ and an integer $k\ge1$. Write $(t^k)$ for $k$ parts equal to $t$ and $(tk)$ for the one-part partition of size $tk$, and read missing parts as zero. Put $s:=n-\nu_1$, with $\nu_1=0$ if $n=0$.

**(i)** Suppose $\lambda_1\le\mu_1\le\nu_1$ and
$$\min\{\lambda_k,\mu_k\}\ge\max\{\lambda_{k+1},\mu_{k+1}\}+s.$$
Then for every integer $t\ge0$,
$$g(\lambda+(t^k),\mu+(t^k),\nu+(tk))=g(\lambda,\mu,\nu).$$
All shifted arguments are partitions of $n+tk$. For $k=1$, this is the first-row padding of the three tails to size $n+t$ ([[def-first-row-padding-of-a-partition]]).

**(ii)** For arbitrary $\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash n$ and $k\ge1$, the sequence $G_k(t):=g(\lambda+(t^k),\mu+(t^k),\nu+(tk))$ is eventually constant. More precisely, it is constant for every integer $t\ge t_0$, where
$$t_0:=\max\{0,\ s+\max\{\lambda_{k+1},\mu_{k+1}\}-\min\{\lambda_k,\mu_k\}\}.$$
The proof of the row-gap identity does not require first-part ordering, so the threshold also covers $k=1$ when $\nu_1<\max\{\lambda_1,\mu_1\}$. No monotonicity is asserted.
items.strategy: Use the locally proved finite LR coefficient identity and first-row Jacobi–Trudi expansion of the reduction lemma directly at the k-row cut. Map alpha to alpha+(t^k), prove the inverse partition and both LR tableau bijections using the sharp s-gap, and compare unchanged small coefficients and tail cofactors. Apply the ordering-free proved identity at t0=max(0,s+max(next rows)-min(kth rows)) to obtain eventual constancy for all k including k=1.
items.axiom_use: None intended: the proof is a direct application of the local reduction lemma and finite ordering of the shifted triple. Re-verify supplier AC status at authoring.

items.title: No general positive combinatorial rule for Kronecker coefficients is known
items.statement:
The results of this page are exact but do not amount to a general positive
combinatorial rule. The definition
([[def-kronecker-coefficient-and-internal-tensor-product]]) computes
$g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ as the multiplicity of a tensor-product decomposition; the
three-character formula
([[prop-kronecker-coefficient-is-a-three-character-inner-product]]) expresses
it as a closed average over $S_n$; the internal product
([[def-internal-product-on-symmetric-functions]]) and the reduction and
row-gap results
([[lem-kronecker-reduction-lemma]],
[[thm-row-gap-reduction-and-conditional-k-stability]]) reduce and stabilize
the coefficient. None of these is a combinatorial interpretation of the
numbers $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$, and no general such rule is known: as recorded by
the sources cited below, obtaining a combinatorial interpretation of, or a
meaningful positive formula for, all Kronecker coefficients is a well-known
open problem in algebraic combinatorics, and the general computation with binary-encoded partition parts is
#P-hard. Panova (2025), Abstract and Introduction (pp. 1–2), also records
the general combinatorial-interpretation problem as open.

**Claim boundary of this page.** This page claims no positive combinatorial
rule for the Kronecker coefficients, no polynomial-time algorithm for
computing them, and no general criterion deciding their positivity. It also
does not claim that such a rule is impossible; the sources record a hard
open problem, not a proved nonexistence theorem.

**Status of the statement.** This is a record of the judgment of the cited
literature, not a theorem proved on this page; it has no proof section and no
items below depend on it as a mathematical supplier.
items.strategy: No proof section. Quote the exact source boundary (Pak-Panova, Bounds, Introduction and Section 7.3: the coefficients themselves are integer and nonnegative by definition but lack a combinatorial interpretation or any meaningful positive formula) and keep the page's claim boundary explicit.

title: Kronecker Coefficients and Internal Products — Examples

items.title: The complete internal product table for S_3
items.statement:
For $S_3$ the three irreducible complex representations are $S^{(3)}$ (the
trivial representation, dimension $1$), $S^{(2,1)}$ (the standard
representation, dimension $2$) and $S^{(1,1,1)}$ (the sign representation,
dimension $1$). Their characters on the three conjugacy classes, indexed by
cycle type in the order $(1^3),(2,1),(3)$, are

| representation | $(1^3)$ | $(2,1)$ | $(3)$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $S^{(3)}$ | $1$ | $1$ | $1$ |
| $S^{(2,1)}$ | $2$ | $0$ | $-1$ |
| $S^{(1,1,1)}$ | $1$ | $-1$ | $1$ |

The complete internal (Kronecker) product table is therefore
$$S^{(3)}\otimes X\cong X\quad\text{for every irreducible }X,$$
$$S^{(2,1)}\otimes S^{(2,1)}\cong S^{(3)}\oplus S^{(2,1)}\oplus S^{(1,1,1)},\qquad S^{(2,1)}\otimes S^{(1,1,1)}\cong S^{(2,1)},\qquad S^{(1,1,1)}\otimes S^{(1,1,1)}\cong S^{(3)}.$$
Equivalently, all Kronecker coefficients $g(\lambda,\mu,\nu)$ with
$\lambda,\mu,\nu\vdash3$ are $0$ or $1$, and the table is invariant under all
permutations of the three arguments. The character table is recomputed here from
the Frobenius dictionary rather than imported from an examples page.
items.strategy: Derive the trivial, standard and sign Specht-character rows, including the sign-twist identification and the two content-(2,1) Kostka counts. Evaluate all ten unordered triples; TTT, TEE, TVV, EVV and VVV have value 1 and the other five have value 0. Symmetry supplies the remaining orders.

items.title: First-row padding below the threshold is undefined
items.statement: For alpha = (2,1) the padded sequence alpha[n] = (n-3,2,1) is a partition exactly when n >= 5. In particular the raw tuples (0,2,1) at n=3 and (1,2,1) at n=4 are not partitions, so the padded family and the padded Kronecker coefficient g_n(alpha,beta,gamma) are undefined below the stated threshold; the padded family for this shape begins only at n = 5.
items.strategy: By the definition of first-row padding, alpha[n] is a partition exactly when n >= |alpha| + alpha_1 = 3 + 2 = 5. For n = 3 the first entry n - 3 = 0 is not a positive part and (0,2,1) is not weakly decreasing; for n = 4 the first entry 1 is smaller than the second entry 2, so (1,2,1) is not a partition. For n = 5 the padded partition is (2,2,1).

items.title: Row padding need not preserve a Kronecker coefficient before stability
items.statement:
**Refuted claim:** adding $t^k$ to the first $k$ rows of the first two
arguments and $tk$ to the first part of the third preserves the Kronecker
coefficient for every $t\ge0$ as soon as the three first parts are ordered
$\lambda_1+t\le\mu_1+t\le\nu_1+tk$
([[thm-row-gap-reduction-and-conditional-k-stability]]).

The witness is $\lambda=\mu=(2,2)$, $\nu=(3,1)$, $k=1$ ($n=4$, $s=n-\nu_1=1$):
$$g\bigl((2,2),(2,2),(3,1)\bigr)=0,\qquad g\bigl((2+t,2),(2+t,2),(3+t,1)\bigr)=1\ \text{ for every }t\ge1 .$$
Thus adding $(t)$ to the first rows does not preserve the coefficient from
$t=0$ on: the row-separation hypothesis of the theorem fails at $t=0$, since
$\min\{\lambda_1,\mu_1\}=2<3=\max\{\lambda_2,\mu_2\}+(n-\nu_1)$. Eventual
constancy is not immediacy.
items.strategy: Compute the coefficients with characters. For t = 0: V_(2,2) (x) V_(2,2) = Sym^2 V_(2,2) + Lambda^2 V_(2,2) = (trivial + V_(2,2)) + sign, and V_(3,1) does not occur, so g((2,2),(2,2),(3,1)) = 0. For t = 1: the triple ((3,2),(3,2),(4,1)) satisfies the conditions of the row-gap theorem with k = 1 (3 <= 3 <= 4, s = n - nu_1 = 1, and min{3,3} = 3 >= max{2,2} + 1 = 3), so the theorem gives g((3+t',2),(3+t',2),(4+t',1)) = g((3,2),(3,2),(4,1)) for all t' >= 0; substituting t = t' + 1 identifies the sequence in the statement. The single value needed is g((3,2),(3,2),(4,1)) = 1: compute the character of S^(3,2) from the permutation module M^(3,2) = S^(5) + S^(4,1) + S^(3,2) (Young's rule; the character of M^(3,2) at sigma counts the 3-element unions of cycles), with chi^(4,1) = chi(M^(4,1)) - chi^(5) (the standard representation), and use the dictionary to get the S_5 character table; the inner product (1/120) sum over the seven cycle types of S_5 gives 120/120 = 1.
